obs: Oklahoma Tax Comm'n v. United States
"It is immaterial that the legislative history of the Act is silent with regard to the tax status of Indian funds."
United States v. United Mine Workers of America

"To find implications in the fact that in the course of the debates it was not explicitly asserted that the district courts could not issue an injunction in a labor controversy even at the behest of the Government is to find the silence of Congress more revealing than the natural meaning of legislation and the history which begot it."
Congress apparently did not discuss the applicability of the Railway Labor Act to a state-owned railroad. This omission is readily explainable
Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co. v. New Jersey Wood Finishing Co.

“there is little in the legislative history to suggest that Congress consciously intended to include… But neither is there any substantial evidence that it consciously intended to exclude… the record… reveals an almost complete absence of any discussion… It seems that Congress simply did not consider the extent of its coverage”

"The committee reports ... and the debates ... make no reference to this change ... In the face of this silence, and without more, ... we are not inclined to read constitutional implications into the absence of the retention provision"
International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. United States
"The legislative history contains no suggestion that any one system was preferred."
Group Life & Health Insurance v. Royal Drug Co.

"That fact fully explains the absence of discussion of such contracts in the congressional debates. Such absence no more indicates a congressional intent to exclude provider agreements from the business of insurance than does the absence of any mention of health insurance companies indicate a congressional intent arbitrarily to exclude all health insurance from the business of insurance."

“Many courts and commentators have observed that the respective legislative histories of § 4 of the Clayton Act and § 7 of the Sherman Act, its predecessor, shed no light on Congress original understanding of the terms business or property. … Nowhere in the legislative record is specific reference made to the intended scope of those terms. Respondents engage in speculation… None of the subsequent floor debates reflect any such intent.”
"Respondents and the Courts of Appeals rely on this failure to respond as indicating an intention ... . We are not persuaded by this negative inference."
“The respondents also rely on what the Committee and the Congress did not say about the 1977 amendments to 307 (b)(1). ... We cannot accept this argument.”

"In fact, the legislative history is silent on the question of whether consecutive sentences can be imposed... Petitioners read this silence as an ambiguity... Petitioners, however, read much into nothing."
"That is because there is no specific legislative history on that phrase to explain what Congress meant."

"We have not been informed of and have not found a single statement anywhere in the legislative history saying that 703(h) does not protect seniority systems adopted or modified after the effective date of Title VII. ... The most which can be said for the legislative history of 703(h) is that it is inconclusive with respect to the issue presented in this case."

"[I]t would be a strange canon of statutory construction that would require Congress to state in committee reports or elsewhere in its deliberations that which is obvious on the face of a statute. In ascertaining the meaning of a statute, a court cannot, in the manner of Sherlock Holmes, pursue the theory of the dog that did not bark."

"With respect to witnesses, the legislative history of the 1866 Act is simply silent, and we are unwilling to assume that, whenever legislators referred to state judicial officials or to the judicial power of the State, they were describing witnesses as well as judges, sheriffs, and marshals."
Block v. North Dakota Ex Rel. Board of University & School Lands

"Recognizing that no express legislative history supports its position, North Dakota relies on congressional silence. ... North Dakota notes the references in the House Committee Report ... to persons, citizens, and individual citizens, and the absence of any references to States."
National Labor Relations Board v. Transportation Management Corp.

"Read fairly, the legislative history does not indicate whether, in mixed-motive cases, the employer or the General Counsel has the burden of proof on the issue of what would have happened if the employer had not been influenced by his unlawful motives; on that point the legislative history is silent."
American Bank & Trust Co. v. Dallas County
“The fact that the 1959 legislative history refers to the Idaho tax, but not specifically to bank shares taxes, does not raise a negative inference limiting the amendment to this specific problem.”
"It also is true that there is no indication in the legislative history that Congress considered the type of transactions involved in this case . . . . The history is simply silent"
"We decline, however, to infer congressional intent to adopt the substance of the Senate version solely on the basis of this legislative silence."
"The House and Senate Reports accompanying the 1976 amendments do not expressly consider what sort of review the district court should perform when no party objects to the magistrates report."
Caplin & Drysdale, Chartered v. United States
"The fact that the legislative history and congressional debates are similarly silent ... means nothing"
Eli Lilly & Co. v. Medtronic, Inc.

"Petitioners principal argument is that the legislative history of 202 mentions only drugswhich is quite different, of course, from its saying (as it does not) that only drugs are included. It is not the law that a statute can have no effects which are not explicitly mentioned in its legislative history . . . . Pittston Coal Group v. Sebben, 488 U. S. 106, 115 (1988)."
“This Court has never required that every permissible application of a statute be expressly referred to in its legislative history.”
“The Courts reliance on the absence of any discussion of foreign convictions in the legislative history is equally unconvincing.”
"the legislative history does not indicate that Congress meant to abrogate such suits. ... (criticizing novel practice of relying on silence in the legislative history) ... (same)"
Arlington Central School District Board of Education v. Murphy

"I concede that sponsors of the legislation did not mention anything on the floor about expert or consultant fees at the time the Conference Report was submitted. ... But I do not believe that silence is significant"

“It says nothing at all about who—judge, jury, or federal safety agency—should decide whether a safer vaccine could have been designed. … Silence cannot tell us to follow those States where juries decided the design-defect question.”

“Even for those Members of this Court who consider legislative history, silence in the legislative history, ‘no matter how ‘clanging,’ ’ cannot defeat the better reading of the text and statutory context… If the text is clear, it needs no repetition in the legislative history; and if the text is ambiguous, silence in the legislative history cannot lend any clarity.”
